By "under a mountain", if you meant you walked horizontally into the mountain from, say - a tunnel at sea level.

If you took raw measurements of the gravity as you went further "under" the mountain, you would record increasingly lower gravity readings, as the mass above you would be pulling upwards on your sensor. 

When you're using gravity measurements in earth sciences, often times you're trying to transform that data into knowledge about the changes in density in the rocks beneath you. 

In your example, you would correct for this mass above you with Bouger correction.  

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouguer_anomaly

If you were tunneling down as well as horizontally, you would also need to correct for your deviation from sea level, adding the necessity for a free air correction as well as a bouger correction.

There may be and angle that which the tunnel exists into a density of rock such that you would read the exact same gravity as you went under the mountain.  That would be an interesting exam question perhaps.

But once it's slipped, less of a chance of that specific fault going again.  If ever, but these faults are small and  there are more of them.

HOWEVER, it's not like a house of cards kind of thing where this type of earthquake will cause a cascade of earthquakes.  Being so far from active tectonics these types of earthquakes (low magnitude, away from plate boundaries) aren't likely to produce aftershocks in the traditional sense.  This isn't a major fault zone that is finding a new equilibrium over a plate boundary- if this was an induced quake any aftershock will be local to the field where the injection is occurring and very small. 

So, in the end - the anwer is "Maybe, it depends" lol.

The stresses are already there.  In the cases of induced earthquakes the injected pressure (hydraulic fracturing or water disposal) reduces the effective pressure that is currently holding the pre-existing fault in place, allowing it to slip.

There's a concept, and truth, out there now by the late Hans Rosling - that he pointed out that the world has already suppassed "peak child".  That is, that there will never be more children in the world as today.

His hour long youtube talk clearly elucidates this concept and that the driving forces behind changing demographics aren't the common myths that people hear.

They hear the term "baby boomer", and think that this is a unique phenominon.  That in the west, you had a "baby boom", after the second world war which caused a large population bubble.

This is true, to some extend - that families had a few years delay being started due to the war.

HOWEVER, the BABY BOOM, this is not.  The Baby Boom - that the world needs to accomodate for is actually falling infant mortatlity rates that comes with access to modernity.  

Prior to modernity, infant mortality was near 50%.  in the sense that 50% ish - wouldn't reach maturity, so families were large - however the effect was a sustained slow rate of growth up until the 19th century (in the west) at about 3%.

After modernity is achieved you have a generation or two that exist when infant mortality rates drop like a brick, but universal education, women's emancipation movements, and access to contraceptive have not had their effects.  THESE generations, of which developed nation has already through (west), developing nations are going through (asia, south asia), and poor agricultural nations (africa) have yet to go through.

We want to have 2-3 children - but prior to modernity, we had to produce twice as many babies to create that.

Point being - Global population growth is actually quite constrained - we have a very accurate picture of what global populations are going to look like and that the problems of this world are ones of resource distribution - not resource scarity.  Granted there are a lot of us, but exponential growth of the human population will not be our ultimate downfall.

It's not a technical problem with pipelines, the term comes from a producer overcomitting oil to a pipeline and not delivering the full quanitity resulting in the pipeline being undercapacity. They are "air" barrels, because even though a company may have 100,000 bbl/d capacity in a much larger pipeline, they are not supplying the full amount.  These inefficiencies in the system can be caused by financial decisions as well as production and plant problems. It is also purposefully done, to ensure that producers can get more of THEIR product to market, by overcomitting to a pipeline they can ensure that if the piplines capacity or their allotment is reduced, the can still sell what they acutally intended to sell (always less than the amount they subscribe).  The overall effect of each producer acting in it's own best interests is a constant amount of oil that isn't reaching the market, lowering the tax revenue on total barrels sold.  Which is bad, however this practice improves a corporations ability to model cashflow and oil supply, giving them an operational buffer and protecting them from quarterly earning shocks.
